items.stem: Which is the definition of the coulomb?
options: The current that flows when 1 V is applied across 1 Ω
The energy transferred per unit current
The charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s
items.answer: The charge passing a point when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s
items.markingKey: Q = It: 1 C = 1 A s.

items.stem: Explain why a lamp lights almost instantly when switched on, although the drift speed of electrons is very small.
items.answer: The wire is already full of free electrons; the electric field is set up throughout the circuit at nearly the speed of light, so electrons everywhere start drifting at once.
items.markingKey: free electrons already present throughout [1]; field established almost instantly [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the drift speed of electrons in a semiconductor is much greater than in a metal for the same current and area.
items.answer: A semiconductor has far fewer charge carriers per unit volume (n much smaller); since v = I/(nAq), v must be much larger.
items.markingKey: n much smaller [1]; v = I/(nAq) [1] [2]

items.stem: A current of 0.25 A flows through an electric motor for 120 s. Calculate the charge that flows.
items.markingKey: Q = It = 0.25 × 120 = 30 C. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A current of 0.60 A flows through a lamp for 1.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows and the number of electrons passing any point in the circuit.

A copper cable of diameter 1.5 mm in a building in Doha carries a steady current of 3.0 A. Copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. (a) Calculate the drift speed. (b) Explain why the cable does not become charged although electrons flow through it.
items.answer: (a) 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ (b) Electrons enter and leave at the same rate; the number of free electrons in the cable stays constant.
items.markingKey: (a) v = I/(nAe) (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 1.25 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ [1] [3] (b) Electrons enter and leave at the same rate; the number of free electrons in the cable stays constant [1]

items.stem: A current of 0.40 A flows for 2.0 minutes. How much charge passes?
Explain what is meant by saying that charge is quantised.
items.answer: Charge exists only in whole-number multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.markingKey: multiples of e [1]; value of e [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the current is the same at all points in a series circuit.
items.answer: Charge is conserved; charge cannot build up anywhere, so the rate of flow of charge past every point is the same.
items.markingKey: charge conserved [1]; no accumulation so same rate everywhere [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the current is the same at all points in a series circuit. (b) Explain what is meant by saying that charge is quantised.
items.answer: (a) Charge is conserved; charge cannot build up anywhere, so the rate of flow of charge past every point is the same. (b) Charge exists only in whole-number multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
items.markingKey: (a) charge conserved [1]; no accumulation so same rate everywhere [1] [2] (b) multiples of e [1]; value of e [1] [2]

items.stem: A silver wire of cross-sectional area 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m² carries a current of 5.0 A. The number of free electrons per unit volume is 5.9 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the drift speed of the electrons.
items.markingKey: v = I/(nAe) = 5.0/(5.9 × 10²⁸ × 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.74 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A aluminium wire of diameter 1.2 mm carries a current of 3.0 A. The number of free electrons per unit volume is 6.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the drift speed of the electrons.

A copper cable of diameter 1.0 mm in a building in Hanoi carries a steady current of 1.5 A. Copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. (a) Calculate the charge passing a point in 60 s. (b) Calculate the number of electrons passing a point in 60 s. (c) State what is meant by a current of one ampere in terms of charge flow.
items.answer: (a) 90 C (b) 5.62 × 10²⁰ (c) One coulomb of charge passing a point per second.
items.markingKey: (a) Q = It: 90 C [1] (b) N = Q/e (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.62 × 10²⁰ [1] [2] (c) One coulomb of charge passing a point per second [1]

items.stem: A copper connecting lead of diameter 1.0 mm carries 1.5 A (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³). (a) Calculate the drift speed. (b) State what is meant by a current of one ampere in terms of charge flow. (c) Explain why the cable does not become charged although electrons flow through it.
items.answer: (a) 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ (b) One coulomb of charge passing a point per second. (c) Electrons enter and leave at the same rate; the number of free electrons in the cable stays constant.
items.markingKey: (a) v = I/(nAe) (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 1.40 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ [1] [3] (b) One coulomb of charge passing a point per second [1] (c) Electrons enter and leave at the same rate; the number of free electrons in the cable stays constant [1]

items.stem: Which is the definition of potential difference?
options: Energy transferred per unit charge from electrical to other forms
items.answer: Energy transferred per unit charge from electrical to other forms
items.markingKey: V = W/Q.

items.stem: Derive P = I²R and P = V²/R from P = VI.
items.answer: Using V = IR: P = I(IR) = I²R; using I = V/R: P = V(V/R) = V²/R.
items.markingKey: substitute V = IR [1]; substitute I = V/R [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why electrical power is transmitted at high voltage.
items.answer: For a given power, P = VI so a higher V means a smaller I; the power lost in the cables, I²R, is greatly reduced.
items.markingKey: higher V, lower I for same P [1]; less I²R loss [1] [2]

items.stem: A filament lamp (at its operating temperature) has a resistance of 48 Ω when connected to a 24 V supply. Calculate the power dissipated.
items.markingKey: P = V²/R = 24²/48 = 12 W. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A resistor has a resistance of 500 Ω when connected to a 9.0 V supply. Calculate the current, the power and the energy transferred in 30 minutes.

A 2000 W, 230 V heater is switched on for 4 minutes. (a) Calculate the current. (b) Calculate the resistance of the element. (c) Explain why the fuse should have a rating just above the normal current.
items.answer: (a) 8.70 A (b) 26.5 Ω (c) It melts and breaks the circuit if the current rises above normal, protecting the cable from overheating.
items.markingKey: (a) I = P/V: 8.70 A [1] (b) R = V²/P (method/substitution) [1]; answer 26.5 Ω with unit [1] [2] (c) It melts and breaks the circuit if the current rises above normal, protecting the cable from overheating [1]

items.stem: Which unit is equivalent to the volt?
items.answer: J C⁻¹
items.markingKey: V = W/Q.

items.stem: Distinguish between electromotive force and potential difference.
items.answer: e.m.f. is energy transferred from other forms to electrical per unit charge (by a source); p.d. is energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge (in a component).
items.markingKey: e.m.f.: other forms → electrical per unit charge [1]; p.d.: electrical → other forms [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp connected in series across the mains do not give their rated power outputs.
items.answer: They are rated for the full mains voltage across each; in series they share the voltage, so each has a smaller p.d. and current, and the power of each is much less than rated.
items.markingKey: voltage shared [1]; smaller power than rated [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why electrical power is transmitted at high voltage. (b) Explain why a 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp connected in series across the mains do not give their rated power outputs.
items.answer: (a) For a given power, P = VI so a higher V means a smaller I; the power lost in the cables, I²R, is greatly reduced. (b) They are rated for the full mains voltage across each; in series they share the voltage, so each has a smaller p.d. and current, and the power of each is much less than rated.
items.markingKey: (a) higher V, lower I for same P [1]; less I²R loss [1] [2] (b) voltage shared [1]; smaller power than rated [1] [2]

items.stem: A power station in Toronto transmits 1.0 × 10⁸ W through cables of total resistance 5.0 Ω at 400 kV. Calculate the current in the cables and the power lost in them, and express the loss as a percentage of the power transmitted.
items.markingKey: I = P/V = 250 A [1]; P_loss = I²R = 3.12 × 10⁵ W [1]; percentage = 0.31% [1] [3]

items.stem: A power station in Mexico City transmits 1.0 × 10⁷ W through cables of total resistance 8.0 Ω at 275 kV. Calculate the current in the cables and the power lost in them, and express the loss as a percentage of the power transmitted.

items.markingKey: (a) R = V²/P (method/substitution) [1]; answer 26.5 Ω with unit [1] [2] (b) Q = It (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2610 C with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the unit of resistivity?
items.answer: Ω m
items.markingKey: ρ = RA/L: Ω × m²/m.

items.stem: Explain the difference between resistance and resistivity.
items.answer: Resistance depends on the material and the dimensions of the sample; resistivity is a property of the material only (R = ρL/A), at a given temperature.
items.markingKey: resistance depends on dimensions [1]; resistivity only on material (and temperature) [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe an experiment to determine the resistivity of a metal wire.
items.answer: Measure the diameter with a micrometer at several points; measure R (V/I with ammeter and voltmeter) for several lengths L; plot R against L; ρ = gradient × A.
items.markingKey: micrometer for d [1]; R for several lengths [1]; graph R vs L [1]; ρ = gradient × A [1] [4]

items.stem: A aluminium wire (resistivity 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) has length 1.0 m and cross-sectional area 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Calculate the resistance of the wire.
items.markingKey: R = ρL/A = 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.0/7.85 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.0357 Ω. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Explain why the resistance of a thermistor (NTC) decreases as its temperature increases.
items.answer: More charge carriers are released as temperature rises, increasing n; this outweighs the increased lattice vibration, so resistance falls.

items.stem: What is the shape of the I-V characteristic of a metallic conductor at constant temperature?
options: Zero current until about 0.6 V, then rising steeply
A curve that flattens at high voltage
A straight line through the origin
items.answer: A straight line through the origin
items.markingKey: Ohmic: I ∝ V.

items.stem: Sketch and explain the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp for both positive and negative p.d.
items.answer: An S-shaped curve through the origin, symmetrical about the origin; the gradient decreases at larger |V| because the filament heats up and its resistance increases.
items.markingKey: S-shape through origin, symmetrical [1]; gradient decreases [1]; resistance increases with temperature [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a diode is used in a mains adapter circuit.
items.answer: A diode allows current in one direction only (low resistance forward, very high reverse), so it converts alternating current to direct current (rectification).
items.markingKey: conducts one direction only [1]; rectification of a.c. [1] [2]

items.stem: For a filament lamp, the current is 0.280 A when the p.d. is 12 V. Determine the resistance of the lamp at this p.d..
items.markingKey: R = V/I = 12/0.280 = 42.9 Ω. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A filament lamp carries 0.15 A at 1.0 V and 0.36 A at 9.0 V. Calculate its resistance at each p.d. and explain the difference.
items.answer: 6.67 Ω and 25 Ω; resistance increases because the filament is hotter at the higher p.d.
items.markingKey: R = V/I: 6.67 Ω [1]; 25 Ω [1]; higher temperature, more lattice vibration [1] [3]

items.stem: Amara investigates the I-V characteristics of a fixed resistor, a filament lamp and a diode in an AS Physics lesson in Lisbon. (a) Draw a circuit diagram suitable for obtaining I-V data, including a way of reversing the p.d. (b) Describe how the graph identifies the diode.
items.answer: (a) Supply with variable resistor or potential divider, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel with component; reverse connections for negative values. (b) No current in reverse; current only above ~0.6 V forward.
items.markingKey: (a) ammeter series, voltmeter parallel [1]; variable supply/potential divider [1] [2] (b) zero current in reverse bias [1]; conducts only above about 0.6 V forward [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the shape of the I-V characteristic of a metallic conductor at constant temperature? (b) Why does the I-V graph of a filament lamp curve?
items.answer: (a) A straight line through the origin (b) The resistance increases as the filament gets hotter
items.markingKey: (a) Ohmic: I ∝ V. (b) Higher temperature → more lattice vibration → higher R; gradient of I-V falls.

items.stem: Explain why it is incorrect to say the resistance of a filament lamp is the gradient of its I-V graph.
items.answer: Resistance at a point is V/I (the ratio of coordinates), not the gradient (which gives ΔI/ΔV); for a non-linear graph these differ.
items.markingKey: R = V/I at that point [1]; gradient is not resistance for curve [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the resistance of a thermistor (NTC) decreases as its temperature increases. (b) Explain the difference between resistance and resistivity.
items.answer: (a) More charge carriers are released as temperature rises, increasing n; this outweighs the increased lattice vibration, so resistance falls. (b) Resistance depends on the material and the dimensions of the sample; resistivity is a property of the material only (R = ρL/A), at a given temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) more charge carriers released [1]; outweighs lattice vibration [1] [2] (b) resistance depends on dimensions [1]; resistivity only on material (and temperature) [1] [2]

items.stem: A student measures the resistance R of different lengths L of a wire of diameter 0.46 mm: L = 0.20 m, R = 0.267 Ω; L = 0.40 m, R = 0.335 Ω; L = 0.60 m, R = 0.402 Ω; L = 0.80 m, R = 0.470 Ω; L = 1.00 m, R = 0.537 Ω. (a) Determine the gradient of a graph of R against L. (b) Calculate the resistivity of the metal. (c) Suggest why the graph has a small positive intercept.
items.answer: (a) 0.337 Ω m⁻¹ (b) 5.60 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m (c) the resistance of the contacts/connecting leads adds a constant to every reading.
items.markingKey: (a) gradient from first and last points = 0.337 Ω m⁻¹ [1] (b) A = 1.66 × 10⁻⁷ m² [1]; ρ = gradient × A = 5.60 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m [1] (c) explanation [1] [4]

items.stem: A constantan wire (resistivity 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m) has length 1.0 m and cross-sectional area 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m². Calculate the resistance of the wire.
items.markingKey: R = ρL/A = 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.0/7.85 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.624 Ω. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: In a college physics laboratory in Bangkok, a 0.80 m length of constantan wire of diameter 0.30 mm is used to find the resistivity of the alloy. (a) State the instrument used to measure the diameter and explain why several readings are taken. (b) Explain why the current should be kept small.
items.answer: (a) Micrometer screw gauge; the wire may not be uniform, and d is squared so its uncertainty matters. (b) A large current heats the wire, increasing its resistance (and resistivity).
items.markingKey: (a) micrometer [1]; non-uniform / averaging [1] [2] (b) heating [1]; resistance changes [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the I-V characteristic of a silicon diode.
items.answer: Almost zero current in reverse bias and in forward bias below about 0.6 V; above this the current rises very steeply with p.d.
items.markingKey: zero in reverse [1]; steep rise above ~0.6 V forward [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the shape of the I-V characteristic of a fixed resistor and explain what it shows about the resistance.
items.answer: Straight line through the origin with constant gradient (constant resistance).
items.markingKey: correct shape [1]; correct link to resistance [1]; explanation of cause [1] [3]

items.stem: For a filament lamp, the current is 0.36 A when the p.d. is 12 V. Determine the resistance of the lamp at this p.d..
items.markingKey: R = V/I = 12/0.36 = 33.3 Ω. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A student is given three unlabelled components and asked to identify them from their I-V characteristics. (a) Describe how the graph identifies the diode. (b) Explain why the resistance of the lamp increases with p.d.
items.answer: (a) No current in reverse; current only above ~0.6 V forward. (b) Higher current heats the filament; increased lattice vibrations impede electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) zero current in reverse bias [1]; conducts only above about 0.6 V forward [1] [2] (b) temperature rises [1]; lattice vibrations [1] [2]

items.stem: Which charge is NOT possible for an isolated object?
items.markingKey: Charge is quantised in multiples of 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5e.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the drift speed of electrons in a semiconductor is much greater than in a metal for the same current and area. (b) Explain why the current is the same at all points in a series circuit.
items.answer: (a) A semiconductor has far fewer charge carriers per unit volume (n much smaller); since v = I/(nAq), v must be much larger. (b) Charge is conserved; charge cannot build up anywhere, so the rate of flow of charge past every point is the same.
items.markingKey: (a) n much smaller [1]; v = I/(nAq) [1] [2] (b) charge conserved [1]; no accumulation so same rate everywhere [1] [2]

items.stem: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ m² carries a current of 3.0 A. The number of free electrons per unit volume is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Work out the drift speed of the electrons.
items.markingKey: v = I/(nAe) = 3.0/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 7.85 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 2.81 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A aluminium wire of diameter 1.0 mm carries a current of 3.0 A. The number of free electrons per unit volume is 6.0 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the drift speed of the electrons.

A copper connecting lead of diameter 1.0 mm carries 2.0 A (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³). (a) Calculate the charge passing a point in 120 s. (b) Calculate the number of electrons passing a point in 120 s. (c) State what is meant by a current of one ampere in terms of charge flow. (d) Explain why the cable does not become charged although electrons flow through it.
items.answer: (a) 240 C (b) 1.50 × 10²¹ (c) One coulomb of charge passing a point per second. (d) Electrons enter and leave at the same rate; the number of free electrons in the cable stays constant.
items.markingKey: (a) Q = It: 240 C [1] (b) N = Q/e (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.50 × 10²¹ [1] [2] (c) One coulomb of charge passing a point per second [1] (d) Electrons enter and leave at the same rate; the number of free electrons in the cable stays constant [1]

items.stem: A heater has a resistance of 20 Ω and a current of 3.0 A. What is its power?
A transmission cable has a constant resistance. The current is multiplied by 4. Explain how the power dissipated in the resistor changes.
items.answer: The power dissipated in the resistor becomes 16 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power dissipated in the resistor ∝ current^2.00; factor = 4.00^2.00 = 16.0. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A heating element has a resistance of 120 Ω when connected to a 230 V supply. Work out the power dissipated.
items.markingKey: P = V²/R = 230²/120 = 441 W. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A power station in Hanoi transmits 1.0 × 10⁷ W through cables of total resistance 4.0 Ω at 400 kV. Calculate the current in the cables and the power lost in them, and express the loss as a percentage of the power transmitted.
items.markingKey: I = P/V = 25 A [1]; P_loss = I²R = 2500 W [1]; percentage = 0.025% [1] [3]

items.stem: An electric kettle in a home in Muscat is rated at 2000 W, 230 V. It takes 4 minutes to boil some water. (a) Calculate the resistance of the element. (b) Calculate the charge that flows. (c) Define the volt. (d) Explain why the fuse should have a rating just above the normal current.
items.answer: (a) 26.5 Ω (b) 2090 C (c) One joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge. (d) It melts and breaks the circuit if the current rises above normal, protecting the cable from overheating.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V²/P (method/substitution) [1]; answer 26.5 Ω with unit [1] [2] (b) Q = It (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2090 C with unit [1] [2] (c) One joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge [1] (d) It melts and breaks the circuit if the current rises above normal, protecting the cable from overheating [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Two wires of the same material and length: X has twice the diameter of Y. The ratio R_X/R_Y is … (b) A wire is stretched to twice its length with its volume unchanged. Its resistance …
items.answer: (a) 0.25 (b) is multiplied by 4
items.markingKey: (a) A ∝ d², so R ∝ 1/d². (b) L × 2 and A ÷ 2, so R = ρL/A × 4.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why it is incorrect to say the resistance of a filament lamp is the gradient of its I-V graph. (b) Describe the I-V characteristic of a silicon diode.
items.answer: (a) Resistance at a point is V/I (the ratio of coordinates), not the gradient (which gives ΔI/ΔV); for a non-linear graph these differ. (b) Almost zero current in reverse bias and in forward bias below about 0.6 V; above this the current rises very steeply with p.d.
items.markingKey: (a) R = V/I at that point [1]; gradient is not resistance for curve [1] [2] (b) zero in reverse [1]; steep rise above ~0.6 V forward [1] [2]

items.stem: A student is given three unlabelled components and asked to identify them from their I-V characteristics. (a) Draw a circuit diagram suitable for obtaining I-V data, including a way of reversing the p.d. (b) Explain why the resistance of the lamp increases with p.d.
items.answer: (a) Supply with variable resistor or potential divider, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel with component; reverse connections for negative values. (b) Higher current heats the filament; increased lattice vibrations impede electrons.
